summary:
Cajamarca has no documented trans-specific regional law, ordinance or incident series in the source inventory; the binding framework is Peru's national legislation, and none of the sources examined contains Cajamarca-specific content.

On 2 April 2025 the plenary of Peru's Congress approved the fused text of the Ley que fortalece el derecho a la indemnidad sexual de los niños y adolescentes and waived a second vote. Its Article 5.1 prohibits any person from entering or using public sanitary facilities designated for a sex other than their birth sex. The same package obliges venues not to post ambiguous restroom signs. The measure had been approved unanimously on 20 February 2025 by the congressional Comisión de Mujer y Familia as a dictamen merging bills 6506 and 8457, sponsored by Jorge Montoya and Alejandro Munante, with narrow exceptions covering custody and cases where required, including accompanying minors, elderly people or people with disabilities.

Enforcement of the restriction falls to individual security staff. Activist Gianna Camacho argues that staff would have to check the DNI to decide whether a woman entering a women's restroom is trans or cisgender, and that the measure is discriminatory. The legislative trigger was a July 2023 complaint over gendered restroom labels at Lima's Jorge Chávez international airport.

Violence against trans people in Peru is documented and rising. The Observatorio de Derechos TLGBI of Universidad Peruana Cayetano Heredia counted 54 killings of LGBTI people and 170 rights-violation cases between 2020 and 2023; 30 of the homicide victims were trans women, 23 gay men and one lesbian, and 19 killings occurred in 2023 alone, 12 of them trans women.

Hate crimes cannot be prosecuted as such in Peru: the state has not incorporated sexual orientation or gender identity into its crime-registration systems.
tangentialFactors:
The human-rights institute IDEHPUCP of the Pontifical Catholic University of Peru, in an analysis of 15 April 2025 by Miriam Tovar and Gonzalo Ugarte, reads Article 5 as a direct breach of equality and non-discrimination under Article 2(2) of the Peruvian Constitution and Article 1.1 of the American Convention on Human Rights, resting on the stereotype that trans people are more prone to enter restrooms to harass or sexually abuse minors.

IDEHPUCP recalls documented cases of trans people barred from public restrooms, including SPC-INDECOPI Resolution 0735-2022, which dismissed a trans woman's discrimination complaint against the gym chain SmartFit after the company grounded bathroom assignment on the sex recorded in the DNI. The institute also records that gender-identity recognition in Peru remains long, costly and invasive.

Unsolved killings dominate the violence record: the killers were not identified in 26 of the 54 homicides, and in 13 of the 19 killings recorded in 2023. In February 2023 the 31-year-old trans sex worker Rubí Torres Silvano was kidnapped from central Lima by the 'Los Gallegos' extortion gang and killed in Carabayllo with some 30 gunshots, days after Priscila Aguado Huatuco, 30, was shot; two killers were arrested in March 2023.
localsOnly:
Peruvian residents seeking legal gender recognition face a process that IDEHPUCP describes as long, costly and invasive, with no streamlined route to amend the DNI.

Because sexual orientation and gender identity are absent from the state's crime-registration systems, residents who are targeted cannot have the motive recorded or prosecuted as a hate crime, whatever the evidence of discrimination.

The national observatory's 2020–2023 count of 170 rights-violation cases sits alongside the 54 killings, and the 2023 total of 19 homicides with 12 trans women victims marks the highest single-year figure in the series.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory reports any trans-specific law, ordinance, enforcement action or incident in Cajamarca itself; whether the department's municipal authorities, private venues or security staff have issued guidance on the national restroom rule is unresolved and not sourced here.

Whether any of the 54 killings or 170 rights-violation cases recorded nationally occurred in Cajamarca is unresolved; the sources break the figures down nationally and by victim profile, not by department.

The full text and current judicial status of SPC-INDECOPI Resolution 0735-2022, and whether it was appealed, are not sourced in this inventory.
